## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}

The statement above is a joke between two logicians (the branch of mathematics that study boolean variables). But almost nobody laughs about it and barely grin when explained. Operations with numbers are natural, however those on logical/boolean variables @sec-boolean are less intuitive. There are essentially two operations: AND and OR.

P1: Is Radama a male? TRUE
P2: Is Radama Malagasy? TRUE

P3: Is Ranavalona a male? FALSE
P4: Is Ranavalone Malagasy? TRUE

The operation with boolean is when we combine P1 and P2,

P5: P1 AND P2
Is Radama a male and Is Radama a Malagasy? Is Radama a Male and Malagasy?
P5 is True

P6: P1 OR P2: Is Radama a male or Malagasy?
P4 is True.

P7: Is Ranavalona a male and Malagasy? P7 is false
P8: Is Ranavalona a male or Malagasy? P8 is true

As of now, P8 is the same as the joke above. Apologies for using strange examples, but we need to exercise our mind, here are a more ecological examples. Essentially we use it to filter dataset. Imaging you ave an excel sheet and have sex in one column (male or female), height in another, and education level (with or without highschool diploma)

We can subset the data by only looking at male with highschool diploma or male or taller. I think the and is more intuitive than the or.

(sex == "male" & education == "with") or male

We use two symbols to represent such operation with.
There is a third symbol, which is !, this negates the proposition, so if P is true then !P is false and vice versa.

Maybe is the that we make illogical decision?

## Examples {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| echo: true

a <- TRUE
b <- TRUE
cc <- FALSE

a | b
a & b
a & cc

a | (b & cc)
(a | b) & cc

# examples with negation
!a


```
